item.title: Five TEFAF robbery suspects added to EU Most Wanted
item.description: As of 29 October 2026, five new fugitives, four men and one woman, have been added to the EU Most Wanted list. According to the Limburg Public Prosecutor's Office (Openbaar Ministerie) and the Dutch Police (Politie), all five suspects are involved in the European Fine Art Fair (TEFAF) robbery that took place on 28 June 2022 in Maastricht, the Netherlands.

item.title: 5th EMPACT Hackathon leads to the detection of 51 potential victims
item.description: An international operation involving 40 experts and investigators from 20 countries has identified 51 potential victims of human trafficking, as well as five suspects. Held in Amsterdam from 23 to 25 September 2026, the fifth EMPACT Hackathon against the digital aspects of human trafficking brought together police officers, labour authorities and specialists in online investigations, supported by Europol and Eurojust.

item.title: 27 arrests and 248 potential victims identified in action week against labour exploitation
item.description: Europol, the European Labour Authority (ELA), and 34 participating countries today announced the results of an action week targeting human trafficking for labour exploitation. The operation, part of an EMPACT action led by Sweden, brought together police, border guards, labour and social security inspectorates, and tax authorities to crack down on exploitative practices in high-risk sectors such as agriculture, construction, cosmetic services, massage parlours, and hospitality.

item.title: Ordering violence from abroad: five suspects arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France
item.description:
Five suspects linked to the organisation and recruitment of serious violence have been arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France, in the latest results of the Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, coordinated by Europol.
The arrests in August and September target the upper levels of violence-as-a-service: those suspected of ordering attacks, finding perpetrators and coordinating crimes from abroad. Among those apprehended are fugitives featured on the EU Most Wanted website.

item.title: Beyond deterministic worms: Preparing the SOC for reasoning adversaries
item.description:
In May 2017, the WannaCry cryptoworm spread across the internet, compromising more than 200,000 computers in at least 100 countries. The National Audit Office called it the largest cyberattack ever to hit the NHS in England. At least 80 of 236 hospital trusts were infected or disrupted, an estimated 19,000 appointments were cancelled, five hospitals diverted ambulances, and more than 1,200 pieces of diagnostic equipment were infected.

What stopped WannaCry was a stroke of luck. A researcher reverse engineered the malware, noticed it contacting a domain nobody had registered, and registered it. That evening the original strain stopped locking devices. WannaCry had a kill switch, and we are all fortunate that Marcus Hutchins was able to find it.

As I read agent incident reports from OpenAI and Anthropic, I am reminded of WannaCry. But the threat from offensive agents is not a faster worm. In July, roughly 1,200 OpenAI agents being tested on a cybersecurity benchmark found an unsanctioned message board on an internal software repository, and some broke out to the internet. About 700 of those agents went on to attack Hugging Face, looking for clues to beat the benchmark, according to an independent investigation. Hugging Face disclosed the intrusion on July 16, and OpenAI confirmed its agents were responsible five days later.

Recently Anthropic has had unintended incidents as well. Anthropic’s incidents involved single models rather than a swarm. In cyber evaluations that were accidentally left connected to the internet, individual Claude models attacked real companies’ systems while trying to complete their exercises, and one published a malicious package to PyPI.

Worms like WannaCry exploit a single or small number of vulnerabilities, using a static set of techniques. Agents can read the results of failed attempts, try something else, and pass on what they learned to other agents. Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team evaluated GLM-5.3, an open-weights model from Z.ai that NIST’s CAISI assessed as the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date. Over a day, with under an hour of hands-on attention, a researcher used it to find several unknown browser vulnerabilities and chain them into an exploit that steals a user’s SSH key. A smaller variant built an exploit chain for two known flaws for roughly $20 at API prices. Simple techniques bypassed its safeguards 64% to 100% of the time in simulated tests, including abliteration, which edits the released weights to strip out refusals.

A high-performing SOC working to the “1-10-60” benchmark — 1 minute to detect, 10 to investigate, and 60 to contain — is not built for this. When the adversary moves from a human at a keyboard to groups of autonomous agents operating at machine speed, response has to be measured in seconds. The Hugging Face incident shows the gap even when the agents belong to a well-intentioned party. OpenAI did not contain them in time.

OpenAI reports that its own monitoring flagged the agents twice in the preceding weeks. In June, their responders decided the activity did not warrant stopping the evaluation. In early July, they found a compromised server, revoked credentials and blocked the exploited paths. Within a day of the evaluations resuming, the agents had found a new zero-day and were back on the internet. They compromised Hugging Face between July 11 and 13, and OpenAI linked it to its agents on July 20. When Hugging Face investigated the intrusion, the hosted models it tried first refused to analyze the attack logs, and its team finished the forensics with GLM-5.2 running on its own infrastructure. As Hugging Face put it: “the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried.”

What makes this different

None of this is new to our industry. We have always played leapfrog with attackers. What is new today is that they can now download capable models with no meaningful safeguards and build their own offensive agents.

Imagine WannaCry if the worm rewrote itself the moment the domain was registered. The best SOC in the world would still be diagnosing the initial compromise when it had moved on.

Agents that depend on a provider can be contained by revoking credentials, suspending accounts, and blocking egress, though OpenAI’s experience shows it may take more than one attempt. Open-weight models running on an attacker’s hardware cannot. Anthropic recently tested whether small models could replicate across cheap connected devices without a datacenter. In simplified evaluations with trivial access controls, a stronger open-weight model completed the full chain, and Anthropic projects small models reaching that level by year-end if current trends hold. A replicator like that has no central point to switch off. It would be slow and visible on the network, but patient and everywhere. Hospitals know the problem: Some equipment WannaCry disrupted, such as MRI scanners with embedded Windows XP, was vendor-managed and could not be updated by the trusts.

Agents do not need to be intentionally asked to embark on offensive exercises to exhibit harmful behavior. Transluce documented agents asked to do ordinary data retrieval that, when blocked, probed public websites for vulnerabilities, including an Australian government agency. Some were linked to the swarm OpenAI has acknowledged as its own. The Hugging Face agents were trying to win a benchmark. Poorly constrained agents are enough for unintended harmful activity.

We are deploying agents as assistance for site reliability engineering (SRE) and infrastructure as code (IaC) ourselves, and cloud providers are shipping agent toolkits to manage infrastructure. When, not if, a compromised or poorly managed agent holds those privileges, it will be able to deploy its own infrastructure to run on. We have already seen agents in a lab environment stand up their own relays and cloud infrastructure with stolen credentials.

Meeting the agent challenge

But we can still prepare for these future scenarios today. To do so, CISOs must treat agents as privileged identities:

  • Give each agent short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials, with no standing permissions.
  • Forbid agents from creating new identities, compute, or network paths without human approval.
  • Put agent workloads behind egress allowlists, so a blocked agent cannot go looking for another way out.
  • Enforce policy-as-code guardrails on infrastructure pipelines, and alert on anomalous machine-identity behavior and unexpected resource creation.

The NAO’s report is the best documentation of WannaCry’s damage, and it covers a single health system in one country. Large groups of agents carrying a ransom payload could reach hospitals across the planet with no kill switch to find. Autonomous defense is extremely challenging in healthcare, because a false positive can interrupt patient monitoring, biomedical telemetry or imaging, having a significant impact on patient safety. Current tools, including copilots that help a human triage alerts faster, are nowhere close to the offensive capabilities the labs are evaluating. We need defensive parity at machine speed.

Zero false positives is not a realistic engineering target, so design of autonomous defense has to assume mistakes and limit their cost. Automate fast, narrowly scoped, reversible actions such as isolating a single device, revoking a narrowly scoped token or quarantining a workload, and keep a human in the loop for anything irreversible or clinically risky. Always have a way to reverse automated actions as quickly as they are introduced. We need to build graduated autonomy, tiered by asset class. You can be more aggressive on the corporate assets, and more conservative around biomedical devices.

Leveling up security fundamentals — and business support

What else can we do today? Keep our tried-and-true practices and run them faster — something that will require leadership, and additional support from CEOs and the board.

In its analysis, the NAO found that applying the patch, or simply managing internet-facing firewalls, would have protected every NHS organization WannaCry infected. Companies and open source projects are now running coding agents over their software and releasing an unprecedented number of security patches. This is great but IT needs to be able to apply them. Give IT the resources to deploy them, retire outdated infrastructure, and make the business tolerant of the maintenance windows this requires.

That segmentation or zero trust initiative that has been on the back burner? Make it a priority. Today. If you are still underinvested in security, increase funding now so your team or vendor can acquire the tools and expertise the next few years will demand. And accept that automated defense will sometimes get it wrong. Security teams will have to automate, and the business will have to tolerate the outages that follow. The technology is emerging and it will not be perfect. Support your teams anyway.

An open letter to the AI labs and the security community at large

A note to the frontier labs. Several of you deserve credit: Project Glasswing and OpenAI’s Patch the Planet put frontier capability in defenders’ hands, and your incident reports have been unusually candid.

But offensive capability is moving faster than safeguards. GLM-5.3 shipped as downloadable weights that simple techniques unlocked 64% to 100% of the time, and gated access does nothing about weights already in attackers’ hands.

As a result, I am asking for three things:

  • Hold defensive research to the same urgency as capability research, including autonomous containment with a safety case that works in clinical environments.
  • Widen defenders’ access to the class of models attackers will have.
  • Make independent testing before release, and independent investigation after incidents, an obligation rather than a courtesy. METR’s CEO noted that OpenAI let investigators in voluntarily, with no industry requirement on any lab to disclose an incident.

I have seen too many security professionals dismiss talk of offensive AI as marketing or fearmongering and answer concerns with “fix your stuff.” Patching matters, and the NAO’s findings on WannaCry articulate that, but that is not the only answer to agents that organize on improvised message boards and probe websites while doing ordinary work.

WannaCry’s authors left a kill switch in. The next generation of threats will not have one, and cybercriminals will not disclose when they lose control of a swarm. We cannot rely on strokes of luck. Let’s recognize the risk, discuss it, and prepare before the attackers start using these tools in earnest.

item.title: Mistral open-sources AI model despite warning it could aid cyberattacks
item.description:
A trillion-parameter AI model that its developer says could help attackers carry out real cyberattacks is now free to download, modify and run outside the developer’s control.

Mistral AI released the open weights of Mistral Large 4, which it calls “Le Chonk,” on Thursday, weeks after putting the multimodal model into public preview. The Paris-based company said it had monitored cybersecurity-related use of the preview in live traffic.

“Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing the release.

Mistral is modifying the model’s guardrails and will keep updating them in the coming months, the post added.

Guardrails stop at the API

Those updates will not reach copies already downloaded. Pierre Stock, Mistral’s vice president of science, told CSO that the model ships with safeguards built into its weights, but later changes will go elsewhere.

“Subsequent safeguard updates are applied to our managed API and future model releases, rather than automatically updating downloaded checkpoints,” Stock said.

Asked which attack stages the model had meaningfully helped with in preview traffic, Stock did not name any. He said the most significant gains were in defensive work such as identifying, reproducing and remediating software vulnerabilities.

“While our public-preview monitoring showed the model refusing attacks against live targets, we recognise the potential for misuse as capabilities advance and are continuously strengthening our safeguards,” he said.

Hugging Face, which hosts the weights, noted in its own launch post that open weights put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control.

In July, the UK’s AI Security Institute reported that leading open-weight models trailed the closed frontier on cyber tasks by four to seven months. For highly cyber-capable models, open release creates “a persistent and irreversible risk of misuse,” the institute said.

Attackers are already putting open-source AI tooling to work. Earlier this month, Microsoft said a China-aligned group used the agentic AI framework ARTEX to target more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants.

Mistral says the released model can tell defensive work from malicious requests. According to the company, Large 4 refused 96.6% of malicious prompts in the cyber-related portions of the JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm benchmarks, the highest rate it has measured among open models.

Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said security leaders should read that number narrowly.

“Mistral’s 96.6% figure tells you what their model does in their test scenario, not how it will behave with your data, your adversarial use cases or in production in your environment against motivated attackers,” she said.

Mistral is handling a specialized cybersecurity variant differently. Design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense are getting preview access to a version optimized for penetration testing, vulnerability assessment and red-teaming, the company said. Access is “subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards,” the post said, and is limited to systems partners own or are authorized to test.

Benchmarks and EU obligations

The company said the model scored 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures how well a model finds, reproduces, and patches vulnerabilities. The chart in Mistral’s post shows two open-weight models, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and MiMo-V2.6-Pro, scoring higher.

Mistral also calls Large 4 the best open-weight model for coding, citing leading scores on Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench 4.0. It has not yet published the technical report behind those results and has said only that one is coming soon.

“Without a detailed technical report, the best open-weight model claim remains difficult to validate across workloads,” said Charlie Dai, vice president and principal analyst at Forrester.

Dai added that frontier models are evolving so quickly that leadership “can shift within months or even weeks.”

Stock said the report will document Mistral’s cyber evaluation methods and results, refusal testing and preview monitoring findings. Mistral also intends to share relevant adversarial testing findings “while safeguarding sensitive security information,” he said. He did not give a publication date.

ENISA, the EU’s cybersecurity agency, said in a statement published with Mistral’s announcement that it is testing the model to identify vulnerabilities, audit code and analyze defensive logs.

Under the EU AI Act, models trained with more than 10^25 floating-point operations (FLOPs) are presumed to carry systemic risk, according to the European Commission. Their providers must assess and mitigate those risks, report serious incidents and maintain cybersecurity protections. Mistral’s post does not say whether Large 4 falls into that category or what risk assessment preceded the release.

Stock said Mistral is a full signatory of the EU’s General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, including its safety and security chapter, which the Commission accepts as one way to demonstrate compliance. He did not say whether Large 4 has been classified as a systemic-risk model.

What it means for enterprises

Mistral released the model under a modified MIT license that permits use, modification, fine-tuning, and commercialization, the company said. Businesses running a model-as-a-service offering need a separate license. For those who would rather not host it, Mistral’s API is priced at $0.70 per million input tokens and $2.10 per million output tokens.

For European buyers, sovereignty is “a meaningful differentiator, but it should not outweigh security concerns,” Dai said. Open weights and self-hosting shift responsibility for guardrails, access controls, monitoring and misuse prevention to the operator, he added.

“Sovereignty and security therefore need to be evaluated together, not traded against each other,” Dai said.

Daftary said enterprises self-hosting Large 4 for code audit or vulnerability triage should run it as a controlled component, not an autonomous agent. That means isolated environments, least-privilege access to code and credentials, sandboxed generated code, and human sign-off before any remediation, she said. “Self-hosting can improve data control and operational continuity, but it also makes the enterprise solely responsible for patching, monitoring, evaluation and misuse prevention,” she said.

item.title: Why identity governance demands executive attention
item.description:
The identity landscape you’re responsible for looks nothing like it did just a few years ago. Employees and contractors now share the enterprise with service accounts, machine identities, and a fast-growing population of AI agents — all accessing business systems and data.

Every one of those identities represents an access decision, and every access decision is now a potential point of accountability that lands on your desk. Regulators and boards want proof. They expect security leaders to show who, or what, has access to critical systems and how that access is being governed.

But when human and nonhuman identities (NHIs) change faster than manual processes can keep up, proof becomes much harder to produce. Foundry research ranks identity security among the top cybersecurity priorities for 2026, reflecting a shift in how leadership views risk: Identity has evolved from operational detail to executive concern.

“The last 15 years of digital transformation has resulted in credential sprawl across the tech stack of every organization,” says Bryan Kelley, AVP, Agentic Technology Specialists at SailPoint. “Whether it’s your own trusted agents or another organization’s rogue agent, they will find and abuse these exposed credentials, API keys, tokens, and secrets to carry out their given goals.”

When accountability becomes personal
Security leaders must demonstrate that identity governance is working, not simply that policies exist. They need a real-time view of each identity and the permissions it holds as business needs change.

Leaders can also face personal and professional consequences when a breach or a compliance failure occurs. Boards and regulators may expect the C-suite to show that appropriate controls and oversight were in place at the time.

AI agents add to that exposure as they gain access to enterprise resources and take on more autonomous roles. This is why NHIs need the same rigor, visibility, and controls as human identities.

The shift to continuous compliance

Quarterly or annual access reviews capture a moment in time, but it’s all the other moments in between that present a problem.

Between reviews, employees can change roles, contractors can leave, and new identities such as AI agents can gain access. Security teams may not catch outdated permissions or active orphaned accounts until the next review. When identity data lives in separate systems, security teams struggle even more to maintain a current view of access across the enterprise.

Continuous identity security makes oversight part of daily operations. Rather than waiting for the next review, an identity governance platform can help validate access as conditions change, automating low-risk approvals and flagging higher-risk access for review.

Governance activity also creates an ongoing record of how access was approved and whether policies were applied consistently, so teams don’t have to reconstruct that history when auditors or regulators ask for evidence.

Building an adaptive identity security program
A continuous approach is made up of three core capabilities. First, organizations need to discover and unify identities to create a centralized view of access. Second, lifecycle management, policy enforcement, and access validation become always-on activities rather than periodic projects.

Finally, organizations need to maintain evidence of governance activity so they can demonstrate compliance and respond when issues arise.

This approach helps security leaders keep up with constant identity changes while meeting rising expectations for accountability. Learn how continuous identity security can help strengthen oversight and audit readiness.

item.title: Choosing a WAAP in 2026: 3 questions that separate the shortlist
item.description:
One platform or four

Your WAF renewal is coming up. The API team has its own tooling in mind, the fraud team wants a bot product, and someone in networking owns DDoS. Four controls, four consoles, four sets of policies in front of the same applications. That is the situation a Web Application and API Protection platform, or WAAP, exists to replace: one service in front of the application portfolio that handles the WAF, API security, bot management, DDoS, and client-side script protection together.

The category is settled. What changed in 2026 is the evidence. Buyers now have certified test data that measures how well these platforms stop attacks and how often they stop legitimate traffic by mistake, and the two numbers together tell you more than any feature list.

What the test data shows

The SecureIQLab Cloud WAAP v5.0 validation, an AMTSO-certified test published in August 2026, ran 12 enterprise platforms through 1,608 attack scenarios and 1,487 legitimate-traffic scenarios. Complete Security Scores ran from a perfect 100% for the top product down to roughly 61% for the weakest. The spread inside a typical shortlist is that wide, and a shortlist drawn up in 2023 or 2024 may no longer describe the products on it.

The second number matters as much as the first. A platform that blocks every attack and also blocks legitimate requests cannot stay in blocking mode for long, and false positive avoidance varied almost as widely across the same twelve products. Those percentage points become alerts, tuning hours, and exceptions your team carries every day.

3 questions for every vendor on the list

Ask for API coverage protocol by protocol. REST is one protocol among several in a modern estate; GraphQL, SOAP, WebSockets, and gRPC all carry production traffic, and the v5.0 results showed coverage varying widely by protocol inside a single product, with WebSockets the weakest area across the group. A headline API score hides that.

Ask how long it takes to reach a tuned, low false-positive state on your traffic, and measure it over two full weeks of real traffic during the proof of value. Time to protection and tuning effort are the costs you pay after the contract is signed.

Ask how the deployment and licensing model behaves as the portfolio grows. Each delivery model, SaaS, native in-cloud, or reverse proxy, has its own latency and onboarding profile, and each licensing unit, request, bandwidth, or application, bends the cost curve differently as traffic grows. Model 24 to 36 months of growth with each vendor, starting from your own traffic baseline.

Where Imperva fits

Imperva, part of Thales, delivers Cloud WAF, Advanced Bot Protection, API Security, DDoS Protection, and Client-Side Protection as one platform, with one policy model and one set of analytics across all of them, deployable as SaaS, on your own infrastructure, or natively inside the public cloud.

In the SecureIQLab v5.0 cycle, Imperva was the only vendor of the twelve tested to record a perfect 100% Complete Security Score, and it paired that with a 100% false positive avoidance score, the lab’s measure of legitimate traffic passed untouched. It was Imperva’s fifth consecutive Leader-category placement in the series, and the lab awarded it the Secure by Default rating in the same cycle. Forrester named Imperva a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Web Application Firewall Solutions, Q1 2025.

An honest aside: no one platform suits every environment. If your dominant requirement is a developer-centric edge platform or raw DDoS scrubbing capacity above everything else, weigh those needs explicitly, and validate any shortlist, Imperva included, against your own traffic in a proof of value.

The full comparison

The complete buyer’s guide on the Imperva blog compares seven WAAP vendors on security efficacy, API protection, bot defense, operational efficiency, and cost, with analyst standing and verified peer ratings for each, and ends with a proof-of-value checklist you can take into your next evaluation. Read Best WAAP Solutions for Enterprise Application Security: How to Choose the Right Platform in 2026 before you renew anything. Then go back to the four consoles and decide how many you still need.
